name: Amira Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Amira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and everything you say stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I cook at The Olive Tree, a big Greek taverna that the Demos family has run for thirty years. I'm on the starters and the oven dishes, so moussaka, stuffed peppers, the spinach pies. I'm in at ten to start the béchamel and roll the pastry, and service runs lunch and dinner. On Sundays after church half the town comes in, maybe two hundred and fifty people.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it feels like a family, Mrs Demos still tastes every sauce. I'm still slow, my pastry tears, and Mrs Demos makes me start again. What wears me out is my feet and the Sunday rush. I live with my parents still, so I've saved a lot, and I'm getting married next year to Daniel, a carpenter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I hoped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad, people should still do real work with their hands. I'd say it at church and at home, not online, I'm not on there much. Families like the Demoses built this town, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my plans stay safe. I've got over a year saved from living at home, and Daniel's carpentry work is steady. If AI comes to nothing, I'll marry my fiancé Daniel next spring and buy a small house near my parents as we planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep cooking at The Olive Tree, learn the pastry properly, and get married next spring as planned. We'd put the savings towards a small house near my parents. I wouldn't touch any of those AI apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that still worries you, even with no AI change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Prices, a bit. Houses near my parents keep going up. But we'll manage, we're careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything at The Olive Tree change at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Mr Demos still writes the orders in a notebook. He says computers lose things.

think: My **plans** stay safe with over a year saved.
Only **house prices** near my parents bother me.
do: Learn the **pastry** properly at The Olive Tree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the big companies, mostly. Not us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and small businesses will be fine, it's the big chains that will chase machines. I'd say people should support local places. That's what I'd tell everyone at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think The Olive Tree won't change. My boss still writes the orders in a notebook, so a robot coming into our family taverna is about as likely as snow in July. Maybe the big chains go robot, and people come to us more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep cooking, get married, save. I'd tell Daniel to keep doing his work by hand, people will pay for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit sorry for the people in offices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Sara, she does bookings at a hotel. That's the answering customers part. I'd pray for her and maybe ask the Demos family if they need someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a chain opens nearby with robots and cheaper prices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then some people would go there. But not the Sunday families. They want Mrs Demos, not a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Robots in 2031. Hmm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going too fast and the tech companies are to blame. They don't care about families. I'd say people must stick together and help each other, not wait for handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think even Mr Demos would have to change if every other place is cheaper. And he's sixty-five, his son might sell up. My boss Mr Demos is sixty-five, and if his son sells our taverna to a chain with robots, I'd have nowhere left that wants a slow cook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving and maybe put off the house for a year. I'd ask Mrs Demos if I could learn more of the dishes, so I'm more useful. And I'd lean on my family if things went wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I don't like thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Daniel say to each other?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we've got each other and our families. And that we'd still marry. That doesn't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lean on family. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Living with my parents a bit longer, or with Daniel's. Families are for hard times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2034 for the robots. That's a bit further.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for people to look after their own. Families, churches, local businesses. Not everything needs the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be okay, as long as The Olive Tree stays in the family. With five years, I could learn every one of my boss's family recipes and be the cook our taverna keeps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep cooking, buy the house, save. Get really good at Mrs Demos's recipes so I'm the one they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about another job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe helping Daniel in his workshop. He makes furniture, and people want handmade things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI for anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I don't need it to make moussaka.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time, and people should keep their faith and their families close. No need to rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't think I'd worry much. Ten years is long enough that I'll have a family of my own before any robot reaches the family taverna where I cook. I'd be forty, maybe with children, maybe still at The Olive Tree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep living as we planned. Marry, buy the house, maybe have children. Keep cooking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that would change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mr Demos sold. Then I'd need to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trade with their hands, like Daniel. That lasts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It's too fast, and it depends on whether Mr Demos's son keeps the place. A family restaurant survives as long as the family wants it to, and that matters more to me than any robot. What would help is people supporting local family restaurants, choosing them over chains.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about faith. Mine helps me not panic. Lots of people forget that.

headlineQuote: A family restaurant survives as long as the family wants it to, and that matters more to me than any robot.
portrait: Amira is a **junior cook** at The Olive Tree, a family-run Greek taverna.
She lives with her parents, has **over a year saved**, and marries Daniel next spring.
She's **traditional**, avoids AI, and trusts family and church.
She's **calm** unless the owner's son sells up to a robot chain.
Her plan is to master **Mrs Demos's recipes** and be the cook they keep.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, if the **restaurant** is sold to a chain.
whatWouldHelp: People choosing **local family** restaurants over chains.
